plain_title: Movement side effects: stiffness, restlessness, tremor
one_liner: Movement problems caused by psychiatric medication, especially antipsychotics: stiffness, tremor, inner restlessness, or involuntary movements.
in_simple_words: Some medications, mainly antipsychotics and a few others, can affect the brain's movement systems. Early effects include muscle spasms (dystonia), stiffness and tremor (parkinsonism), and an awful inner restlessness (akathisia). Tardive dyskinesia is a later effect: repetitive involuntary movements, often of the mouth, tongue, or limbs, that can persist. These aren't signs of the illness getting worse. Tell your prescriber early; most effects can be reduced by adjusting the medication or adding treatment.
what_it_can_feel_like: I couldn't sit through a meal. I paced and paced and thought I was losing it. It was akathisia, and a dose change fixed it in days.
My mum's mouth moved constantly and nobody at the home mentioned it. A new psychiatrist spotted tardive dyskinesia straight away.
common_signs: Painful muscle spasms of the neck, jaw, or eyes soon after a dose change
Stiffness, slowness, shuffling walk, or tremor
Intense inner restlessness; needing to pace or shift constantly
Repetitive involuntary movements of the mouth, tongue, face, or limbs that develop over time
Movements that other people notice before you do

myths_vs_facts.myth: Restlessness or stiffness means the mental illness is getting worse.
myths_vs_facts.fact: These are usually medication effects, and they're treatable. Mistaking akathisia for agitation can lead to dose increases that make it worse.

myths_vs_facts.myth: Tardive dyskinesia is untreatable, so there's no point mentioning it.
myths_vs_facts.fact: Catching it early gives the most options, and newer medications specifically treat it. Always mention new movements.

myths_vs_facts.myth: You should stop the medication if you notice movements.
myths_vs_facts.fact: Stopping suddenly can be dangerous. Tell your prescriber and decide together; adjustments are often enough.

how_common.plain: Around 1 in 4 people on long-term antipsychotics has some tardive dyskinesia, with lower rates on newer medications. Akathisia and parkinsonism are common early on.
how_common.figure: Tardive dyskinesia mean prevalence 25.3% (20.7% on second-generation, 30.0% on first-generation antipsychotics; meta-analysis of 41 studies, 2000–2015)

what_helps.plain_summary: Your prescriber may lower the dose, switch to a medication less likely to cause movement effects, or add a medication that counters the effect. Akathisia often responds to dose changes and specific add-on medications. Tardive dyskinesia can be treated with newer medications (VMAT2 inhibitors) in some countries, alongside review of the antipsychotic. Regular movement checks, ideally every few months, catch problems early. Never stop or change doses on your own.
evidence_based_options: Dose reduction or switch to a lower-risk antipsychotic, with your prescriber
Add-on medication for dystonia, parkinsonism, or akathisia, prescribed and monitored by a doctor
VMAT2 inhibitors for tardive dyskinesia where available, prescribed and monitored by a doctor
Regular structured movement monitoring (for example, the AIMS check)
self_help_that_supports_care: Telling your prescriber about any new movement, stiffness, or restlessness
Asking for a movement check at each review
Keeping a short note or video of movements to show the clinician
Peer groups where people share what helped

when_to_reach_out: Tell your prescriber as soon as you notice stiffness, tremor, restlessness, or involuntary movements. Seek urgent care for a sudden painful spasm of the neck, jaw, eyes, or throat, or any trouble swallowing or breathing, which can be acute dystonia and is treatable quickly.
is_not: Movement problems from Parkinson's disease, Huntington's, tics, anxiety, or other medical conditions are assessed separately. Agitation from the illness itself can look like akathisia; the difference matters for treatment.
hope_note: Most movement effects can be reduced or managed. Being heard by a prescriber who checks regularly makes all the difference.

content_notes: Site-wide crisis link stays one tap away.
No doses or tapering schedules given; always 'with your prescriber'.

sub_sections.title: Acute dystonia
sub_sections.text: Sudden muscle spasms within days of starting or increasing a dose. Treated quickly with medication.

sub_sections.title: Akathisia
sub_sections.text: Inner restlessness and the need to keep moving. Often mistaken for anxiety or agitation.

sub_sections.title: Drug-induced parkinsonism
sub_sections.text: Stiffness, tremor, slow movement, reduced facial expression.

sub_sections.title: Tardive dyskinesia
sub_sections.text: Involuntary repetitive movements that develop after months or years and may persist.
